entries.title: Armed Man Arrested at Trump’s LA Golf Course Ahead of the President’s Visit
entries.summary: Deputies found a loaded pistol with a 16-round magazine containing hollow-point ammunition on the man, the sheriff’s office said.
entries.content:
A heavily armed man was arrested at President Donald Trump’s golf course in Los Angeles days before his Tuesday fundraiser there, authorities said.

Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department deputies detained Jeanine John Taele, 38, on Sunday after he was seen taking photos and “appearing to monitor security-planning activities” at the Trump National Golf Course in Rancho Palos Verdes, the sheriff’s office said.

Taele was arrested on suspicion of carrying a concealed firearm and possessing prohibited ammunition after the deputies found a 16-round magazine containing hollow-point ammunition tucked into his pants, along with a loaded pistol and additional ammunition in his car, according to a statement from the sheriff’s office.

Deputies later searched his residence and found an illegally modified AR-style rifle, body armor, more high-capacity magazines and notebooks consisting of “concerning statements.” The deputies also discovered that Taele was under investigation for robbery by the El Segundo Police Department, the sheriff’s office said.

Trump was aboard Air Force One on his way to speak at a Republican National Committee fundraiser at the golf course when authorities first announced the arrest Tuesday afternoon.

The FBI’s Joint Terrorism Task Force and the Secret Service are investigating, but authorities have determined there is “no credible threat,” the sheriff’s office said. The Secret Service did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
entries.author: Torrie Herrington

entries.title: Missouri Elections Official Blocks Petition Challenging GOP-Friendly Redistricting Map
entries.summary: Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins said the petition had the requisite number of signatures but was still “unconstitutional.”
entries.content:
Missouri’s top elections official squashed a challenge to Republicans’ new congressional map that could net them one more U.S. House seat, waiting until the last possible day to block a petition that would have triggered a statewide vote on the gerrymander.

Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, on Tuesday rejected petitioners’ attempt to put the map on the ballot in November ahead of the deadline to decide whether the petition could advance, saying the challenge itself was “unconstitutional.”

“At issue is not the number of signatures turned into the challenge, the new congressional map, but the fact that the referendum itself is null and void by virtue of the fact that it is unconstitutional,” Hoskins said at a Tuesday press conference. “Therefore, House Bill 1, the Missouri First map, continues to be the law of the land.”

Hoskins also said that Gov. Mike Kehoe and Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway agreed with his choice. At the press conference, Hoskins said he was “confident in the stance” he's taken, and that the government is “prepared to go to court.”

That chance will come soon: People Not Politicians Missouri, the group that led the original petition, confirmed in a statement Tuesday evening that it plans to announce details regarding future litigation tomorrow.

The Missouri General Assembly pushed through a new map targeting Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s heavily Democratic district, becoming one of the first states that moved to redistrict after President Donald Trump pushed state lawmakers to redraw their congressional maps to more heavily favor Republicans.

Signed into law by Kehoe last September, the map carves Missouri’s largest city, Kansas City, into three congressional districts.

Shortly after the assembly pushed the new lines through last fall, People Not Politicians Missouri gathered over 300,000 signatures to force a referendum. In Missouri, a petition with enough signatures triggers a veto referendum, or a statewide vote on the law in question.

The group filed the signatures in December. Hoskins had until 5 p.m. Tuesday to decide on the legality of the petition — the same day as Missouri’s primary elections.

Hoskins was widely expected to not certify the signatures, previously saying that any signatures gathered before the campaign was approved by his office constituted “a misdemeanor election offense,” a claim his office later clarified and corrected.

“Secretary of State Hoskins is making a last desperate attempt to silence the people’s voice in Missouri,” Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, wrote in a statement. “We’ve fought back against politicians for the last year, and we won’t stop now. There are more than enough signatures, verified by election authorities, to qualify the referendum.”

entries.title: HHS Awards Small Texas Firm With $150M Contract to Represent Unaccompanied Children
entries.summary: The Burke Law Group could now be tasked with representing over 20,000 children in immigration proceedings.
entries.content:
The Department of Health and Human Services revealed plans to award a multimillion-dollar contract to a small Texas law firm, tasking it with representing thousands of immigrant children as they face immigration court proceedings.

HHS’s refugee resettlement division — charged with overseeing unaccompanied undocumented children — had a contract with the Acacia Center for Justice that was not renewed after expiring last Friday. The federal government had a fraught relationship with Acacia, including attempting to terminate its legal contract last March and withholding funding for months. Nonprofits have sued to get the agency to pay invoices dating back to December totaling roughly $65 million, the groups announced last week.

On Thursday, Acacia said its legal teams had defended more than 20,000 children despite not being paid. In a Tuesday statement before the new contract was published, the organization said it was “adamant” whoever took over the contract must have “deep experience” with the country’s immigration system.

The Office of Refugee Resettlement quietly awarded the new contract — worth up to $150 million per year — to the Burke Law Group, a boutique law firm headquartered in Houston. No one at the organization specializes in immigration law, according to staff biographies on the website, though the site lists “immigration and asylum” as one of two-dozen practice areas on a separate page.

The firm would “provide legal orientation, legal consultation and attorney-of-record representation services” for unaccompanied immigrant children while under Office of Refugee Resettlement care, the agreement reads, and help connect them with legal resources after being discharged. The federal government has been required to help facilitate legal counsel for unaccompanied children in Office of Refugee Resettlement custody since 2008.

Founder and managing partner Marcella Burke worked in President Donald Trump’s first administration, serving as deputy general counsel in the Environmental Protection Agency before moving to the Department of the Interior, according to her LinkedIn profile. She is also a board member for the Federalist Society Houston Lawyers Chapter, according to a release noting her appointment by Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to the Texas School Land Board.

“The purpose of this proposed award is to provide legal orientation, legal consultation, and attorney-of-record representation services for eligible unaccompanied children (UACs) during immigration proceedings,” the notice, which is set to be officially published on the Federal Register on Thursday, read.

The contract is set to go into effect on Aug. 15 and last one year.
entries.author: Manuela Silva

entries.title: Chuck Edwards Ends His Reelection Following Harassment Allegations
entries.summary: The House Ethics Committee had recommended the North Carolina Republican be censured.
entries.content:
Rep. Chuck Edwards suspended his campaign for reelection early Wednesday morning following a House Ethics report that cited alleged inappropriate behavior toward two women staffers.

“After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign,” he posted on X. “I will complete my current term. Serving Western North Carolina has been the honor of my life. Thank you for your trust, prayers, and support. God bless WNC and America.”

The Ethics committee recommended on Monday that the North Carolina Republican be censured and found “substantial reason to believe Representative Edwards violated House Rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces,” according to a committee press release.

Edwards was running for reelection in North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District, one of two competitive districts in the state crucial to both parties’ path to a majority in Congress.

Pressure had been building among Republicans to force him out.

House Republicans were privately trying to convince Edwards to abandon his reelection bid in light of the House Ethics committee’s report, CNN reported on Tuesday. A source on Capitol Hill told The News & Observer that Sen. Ted Budd (R-North Carolina) asked Edwards to drop out of the race.

A spokesperson for Budd told NOTUS on Tuesday that while the senator doesn’t disclose his private conversations, he “finds the House Ethics report deeply concerning.” The spokesperson added that Budd "believes Rep. Edwards faces a significant uphill battle in his reelection bid,” pointing to Edwards’ trailing poll numbers and that his opponent is vastly outraising Edwards.

Since Edwards withdrew from the race before military and overseas absentee ballots were distributed on Sept. 4, state law says the North Carolina 11th District GOP Executive Committee, which includes the district party’s officers as well as other members, can choose Edwards’ replacement on the ballot.

The House Ethics Committee found that Edwards gave the two women staffers “lavish gifts,” including expensive jewelry, designer purses, vacations, guns, and dinners.

The report also pointed to instances when Edwards paid for spa trips, talked to staffers about going to D.C. strip clubs, and told one of the staffers not to let his scheduler know about a dinner the two had planned.

The committee did not find evidence that Edwards “engaged in sexual activity with or explicitly propositioned any individual under his employ.” The report said that Edwards was aware that his “excessive attention toward the young women had led to rumors and innuendo in the office” and “acknowledged at least some of the behavior at issue could be viewed as inappropriate.”  

Even before news broke about him being the subject of a House Ethics investigation in May, Edwards faced a competitive challenge from Democrat Jamie Ager, a farmer backed by the centrist group Blue Dog Democrats who comes from a family of North Carolina politicians.

Ager is one of several Democrats running in red districts that have the backing of House Democrats’ campaign arm through its Red to Blue program. The Cook Political Report changed the district’s rating from “Likely Republican” to “Lean Republican” in June.

The state’s other competitive seat is North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, currently held by Democrat Rep. Don Davis.

entries.title: The Key Economic Warning Sign That Could Upend the Midterms
entries.summary: Turbulence in the bond market is near levels where “things start to break,” economists warn.
entries.content:
When President Donald Trump suddenly backed off his massive “Liberation Day” tariffs in April 2025, he acknowledged his reversal had been driven by one factor in particular: “I was watching the bond market. The bond market is very tricky … People were getting a little queasy.”

Over the past week, the bond market has looked more than a little queasy. The deterioration of arguably the most critical financial asset in the world now risks rippling through the broader U.S. economy in dangerous and unpredictable ways — and possibly right before the 2026 midterm elections.

On Friday, the yield on the 30-year Treasury bond reached a nearly two-decade high of 5.3%, and has only partly come back down since then. The yield on the 10-year Treasury bond spiked above 4.7% — the highest level since the beginning of the Trump administration. It recovered on Monday and Tuesday, but remains near recent highs.

“Five percent is really when things start to break,” said Joseph Brusuelas, principal and chief economist for RSM US LLP, of the 10-year Treasury bond yield. “You don’t know where it’s going to be. But if rates surge, it’s going to cause some problems in those institutions. And then who knows what can go wrong next.”

Economists and Wall Street analysts generally agree that the risks to small- and medium-sized banks grow substantially if 30-year Treasury bond yields rise above 6% and 10-year Treasury bond yields rise above 5%. They say both numbers are worryingly within reach.

The last sustained period of high interest rates led to the failure of Silicon Valley Bank, precipitating a bailout from the Biden administration to prevent a broader financial contagion from dragging down the U.S. economy.

The $40 trillion in outstanding debt issued by the federal government is a pillar of the global economy. The 10-year U.S. Treasury bond is the benchmark for mortgage rates, housing loans, credit card payments and a host of other critical functions, in addition to serving as the reserves for countries around the world. Already high borrowing costs have made it more expensive to take out a mortgage, buy a car or start a business, and have also driven up the costs to taxpayers of financing the debt.

Trump's been feeling the squeeze: his approval rating on the economy dropped from 38% to 30% from March to April, according to an Associated Press poll. Democrats’ approval ratings generally are also abysmal, but they should benefit if voters take out their anger over the economy on the president — especially if new problems emerge in the next three months.

On Wednesday morning, the Treasury Department will announce plans for later Treasury auctions to borrow an additional $739 billion to fulfill government payments between July and September. This will be a key gauge of investors’ appetite for buying more U.S. debt despite the recent concerns. Any shortage of investor appetite could trigger another sharp rise in bond yields.

“Between now and the midterms, probably the biggest risks are some kind of failed Treasury auction,” said Adam Posen, president of the Peterson Institute for International Economics, a centrist think tank. “It’s like so many other things where people adapt and reset expectations because the world didn’t end last time, so I won’t overreact this time. That’s only true until it isn’t.”

Trump’s declared “Liberation Day” tariffs triggered a financial market panic in which investors dumped billions in U.S. treasuries. Faced with the broad economic fallout of the bond market crisis, Trump suspended most of his import duties at the last moment. Markets recovered with relative ease.

The spike this time was less sudden and has gotten less attention. But it may also be harder to resolve.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh last week fueled doubts about the central bank’s willingness to hike interest rates to fight inflation. This drove investors out of long-term bonds, because out-of-control inflation reduces the value of the dollar over time. Warsh has been under pressure from Trump not to raise interest rates because they slow down economic growth.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Tuesday expressed optimism that prices are generally heading in the right direction, which would put less pressure on Warsh to raise interest rates. But other economists have been skeptical, noting that inflation remains well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target.

“What gives me the confidence is that the underlying numbers — they are very tame,” Bessent said on CNBC. “I think we're going to continue to see that.”

Even if Warsh can preserve the central bank’s inflation-fighting credibility, there may be other threats to the bond market that could prove harder to untangle than calling off the “Liberation Day” tariffs.

Japan is the second-largest holder of U.S. treasuries in the world, with $1.1 trillion in holdings. But Japan has faced a severe currency crisis of its own, and moved to sell treasuries to prop up the value of the yen, in turn putting further pressure on U.S. bonds. Bessent stepped in this week to prop up the yen, and while that effort has looked successful thus far it may prove a temporary salve.

An escalation in hostilities with Iran could also lead to another surge in bond yields. Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWD Bonds, said “the big swings” in oil prices tied to the resumption of fighting have been perhaps an even greater cause of volatility, as investors rush to beat the market. Bonds calmed after Trump's latest comments over the weekend that a deal with Iran was within reach, but then the president has also threatened the country with "decapitation" if it did not accept an agreement.

Even without the war or spillover from Japan, analysts say high yields will persist as long as the federal government continues to run annual deficits that are close to 6% of the national economy. While large deficits are unlikely to cause a market crisis, particularly in the short term, the fiscal imbalance still drives higher rates that raise borrowing costs for the government and therefore U.S. consumers.

“My view of the most likely scenario is that we have no acute crisis, but rates stay high in a way that is still a really big problem — the cost of homeownership continues to be a disaster, and consumers face high interest rates,” said Tobin Marcus, the head of U.S. policy and research at Wolfe Research and a former Biden economic official. “It’s a little hard to tell a story about a major catalyst where something big breaks, but it’s definitely possible.”

The odds of a deal to lower the deficit are vanishingly small, and that means the pressure will likely fall primarily on the Federal Reserve not to reprise last week’s disaster. If it cannot do so between now and November, the political impact may be felt sooner rather than later.

“If the concerns with the Fed grow, what we see with interest rates will just keep going higher,” said Claudia Sahm, a former economist with the central bank. “And regular people will notice that.”
entries.author: Jeff Stein

entries.title: Freedom 250 Sponsors Failed to Disclose Donations — A Potential Lobbying Law Violation
entries.summary: Corporate giants such as Lockheed Martin, ExxonMobil and United Health Group could run afoul of the Lobbying Disclosure Act.
entries.content:
The Great American State Fair was covered in the logos of dozens of corporate lobbying giants.

But most of the event sponsors — including defense contractors Lockheed Martin, GE Aerospace and Northrop Grumman — did not disclose payments to the President Donald Trump-supported event organizer Freedom 250, in potential violation of federal lobbying law, according to a NOTUS review of federal lobbyist contribution reports due to Congress by last Friday.

The Great American State Fair was also “presented by” corporate giants including ExxonMobil, SAP, Exiger, Mosaic and ScottsMiracle-Gro, according to billboards NOTUS photographed around the fair grounds last month. They’re among the almost two-dozen companies, including Palantir, Oracle, UnitedHealth Group and John Deere, listed as “sponsors” on the Freedom 250 website.
LockheedMartin.State.Fair (4722x2656, AR: 1.78)Only three Freedom 250 corporate sponsors — Chevron, United Airlines and RTX — disclosed financial contributions to the organization as required by the federal Lobbying Disclosure Act. Ethics experts told NOTUS that the other companies should, too.

Under the Lobbying Disclosure Act, any entity that lobbies the federal government must file semiannual reports with Congress detailing honorary expenses, event cost payments and donations to political campaigns, presidential inaugurations, presidential libraries and other entities established or controlled by public officials.

The law “is certainly not airtight, and certain entities have found ways to try to exploit this law,” Aaron Scherb, a longtime ethics and democracy advocate, told NOTUS.

“Nonetheless, it requires full disclosure of political spending when companies are trying to curry favor with an administration and elected officials,” Scherb added. “So, companies contributing to Freedom 250 should absolutely be required to disclose their political spending.”

Freedom 250 was established by Task Force 250, which Trump created via executive order.

Trump himself is the chair of Freedom 250. The limited liability corporation is housed within the National Park Foundation, the nonprofit charity arm of the National Park Service, to which companies have previously disclosed donations.

“When it comes to other nonprofits, the question is always whether it was created and controlled by Trump,” Craig Holman, a government affairs lobbyist at the left-leaning nonprofit watchdog Public Citizen, told NOTUS. “But there is little question about Freedom 250.”

The offices of the clerk of the House and secretary of the Senate, which are tasked with processing lobbying disclosures and questioning lobbyists who fail to comply with reporting requirements, did not respond to requests for comment on obligations to disclose contributions to Freedom 250. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, which is tasked with enforcing compliance, also did not respond to questions.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Freedom 250 had raised $50 million from a variety of corporate interests. But the vast majority of these reported contributions — including $2 million from TikTok and $1 million each from Oracle and ExxonMobil — were not separately disclosed in certified federal disclosures, as required by the Lobbying Disclosure Act.

As of Tuesday evening, only three companies that both lobby the federal government and contributed money to Freedom 250 disclosed how much they gave to the Trump-backed organization.

Oil company Chevron, a presenting sponsor of the Great American State Fair, shelled out $5 million in May, according to federal records first reported by Politico and Sludge.

United Airlines disclosed donating $2.5 million in March.

And RTX, the defense company formerly known as Raytheon, reported giving $1.5 million in May.

Chevron, United Airlines and RTX are among the nearly two-dozen corporate sponsors listed on the Freedom 250 website.

“As a proud American company, Chevron is pleased to support celebrations of 250 years of the country's independence,” Bill Turenne, a spokesperson, told NOTUS.

United Airlines declined to comment. RTX did not respond to a request for comment.

A spokesperson for Palantir, one of the companies listed as a sponsor on the website, told NOTUS the company did not donate to Freedom 250.

“Palantir is proud to adhere to all lobbying and donation disclosure requirements, but the company did not make a contribution to Freedom 250,” the Palantir spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement.

GE Aerospace declined to comment. UnitedHealth Group, John Deere, Lockheed Martin, TikTok, Oracle, ExxonMobil, Northrop Grumman, ScottsMiracle-Gro, Exiger, Mosaic and SAP did not respond to requests for comment from NOTUS.

Other companies not listed by Freedom 250 as official partners or sponsors said they did not pay the organization money despite having their corporate logos posted around the Great American State Fair.

Axiom Space had an exhibit that included a video and a large astronaut cutout. But Meridyth Moore, a spokesperson for Axiom Space, said the company “was not a paid sponsor.”
Axiom.Space (8064x4536, AR: 1.78)"That’s it. We provided a cutout image of our spacesuit and a video to be played,” Moore responded when asked for more details about the exhibit.

When NOTUS asked if the organizers had allowed Axiom to include the pieces for free, Moore confirmed “no expenditures were spent.”

Hillsdale College, a small, Christian liberal arts school in Michigan, also had a branded booth at the Great American State Fair. Emily Davis, a college spokesperson, described Hillsdale as a “partner” but said the college did not donate to Freedom 250.

“The college complies with all reporting obligations. It has not given any monies to the Freedom 250 group,” Davis said.

SAP, a business software company, operated a large exhibit at the Great American State Fair, which included a display wall featuring the logos of several client companies alongside QR codes and a rotating digital display detailing some of the brands.
SAP.ads.Great.American.State.Fair (8044x4525, AR: 1.78)Todd Scott, senior communications manager at Hershey, one of the companies featured in the SAP exhibit, told NOTUS that the chocolate company was not a sponsor and that this was the first he had heard about the company’s logo being on the SAP exhibit at the Great American State Fair. (NOTUS reported on Hershey’s presence at the Great American State Fair in July.)

Scott pointed to an article in The Philadelphia Inquirer, where he previously said Hershey was “asked so late in the game” to participate in the Great American State Fair that the company could not logistically participate.

Funding for Freedom 250 has often lacked transparency since the group began operating alongside America250 — a separate nonprofit group supporting the U.S. Semiquincentennial Commission, which Congress established a decade ago.

Oil company BP, for one, disclosed a $500,000 contribution to America250 in February, according to its latest contribution report filed last Friday.

Democrats on the House Natural Resources Committee accused Freedom 250 of diverting funds from America250, including by allegedly giving donors the routing and account numbers for Freedom 250, according to a report released by the committee last month.

Freedom 250 spokesperson Danielle Alvarez previously told NPR that the claims are "categorically false” and a "partisan smear."

"Congressional members should be ashamed they are spending countless hours fabricating a report instead of joining Americans in creating an absolutely beautiful celebration," Alvarez told NPR last month.

Alvarez did not immediately respond to a NOTUS message following up on questions emailed separately to Freedom 250.
entries.author: Taylor Giorno

entries.title: Do the Commanders have a problem at center?
entries.summary: With presumed starter Nick Allegretti sidelined, the position has drawn attention early in camp.
entries.content:
Things are looking a little dicey at the center of the Commanders’ offensive line.

The team’s presumed starter at the center position is actually a converted guard. His backup is also a converted guard. The rookie they drafted in the sixth round of April’s draft — a converted guard. The center they signed earlier this week to fill in due to injuries? You guessed it.

As the Commanders make their way through the second week of training camp, the centers have drawn a fair amount of attention. With the offense seeking to rebound from a bottom-10 performance last season, it's unclear what one of the unit’s most important positions will look like next week, let alone next month.

Coach Dan Quinn isn’t in panic mode. Despite the absence of starter Nick Allegretti due to a calf strain, Quinn said the offensive line has held up.

“Both sides of the line I thought had, you know, advantage here, advantage there, and that's what I'm hoping to see,” he said ahead of practice Tuesday. “If one gets tilted too much to the other, then I'd be more concerned. So I like the back-and-forth, honestly, to say good run here, good blitz there.”

Despite Quinn’s optimistic take, there are still plenty of question marks. Allegretti has not practiced since July 29. His backup, Julian Good-Jones, has had an up-and-down run as fill-in with the first team, including one snap that went over Jayden Daniels’ head during team drills on Tuesday. Rookie Matt Gulbin has rolled almost exclusively with the second team, but depth is clearly a concern.

The team worked out centers Gus Hartwig, Joe Michalski and Trey Hill on Saturday. Hill, a sixth-round pick by the Bengals in 2021 who played guard early in college, was signed the following day. Following Saturday’s and Monday’s practices, guards Timothy McKay and Brandon Coleman and tackle Trent Scott stayed to take snaps with Marcus Mariota.

Quinn said all the maneuvering has been aimed at building depth (before Hill’s arrival Gulbin was the only player on the team roster listed as a center), but is also an experiment to see who is capable of handling center responsibilities.

“If you can play inside, you want somebody that can play both [center and guard],” Quinn said. “And that's basically kind of the rhythm behind it.”

The center position is pivotal to the offense. The job isn’t solely about successfully snapping the ball to the quarterback. Centers are responsible for calling out defensive alignments, coordinating blocking assignments and, of course, handling the defender in front of them.

And yet Washington has not had consistency at the position for years. Since 2021, at least 10 players have taken snaps at center for Washington. Last season, the offensive line was just about average in ESPN’s pass- and run-block metrics, and that was before starting center Tyler Biadasz was released in February.

Quinn has commended Gulbin for his command of the second unit line.

“I think it's just kind of a next-man-up mentality,” Gulbin said. “I have to step up to the plate and make sure the O line's functioning, and I'm getting out calls.”

Allegretti has helped coach up Good-Jones and Gulbin from the sideline. Those three, and now Hill, can be seen bouncing ideas and techniques off one another. After practice they often put in extra work with assistant offensive line coach Shane Toub.

“I come off the sideline, he's [Allegretti’s] helping me out with ‘Oh, what was this? What was this look?’ We break it down together,” Good-Jones said. “So it's a brotherhood, man. It's a collaborative unit.”

Quinn has said he doesn’t expect Allegretti to be out much longer. And even though the seven-year veteran started just one game at center for Washington last season, his teammates, the coaching staff and front office have raved about him.

“What stands out to me with Nick is just his leadership, his command, his confidence, the way the guys gravitate to and listen to him,” general manager Adam Peters said at a press conference before camp. “And so that's a big part of it. Knowing what to do, knowing where to go, knowing where to direct the guys, just the calling up in the huddle — it's a big deal.”
entries.author: Martenzie Johnson

entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (Aug. 7)
entries.summary: The grand opening of Olney Theatre’s expansion, a sitcom-inspired dance party, and a canine competition at the Wharf.
entries.content:
Thursday

“Woody Guthrie’s American Song,” Theatre Alliance at Wharf Park
515 Water St. SW, 7:15 p.m., pay what you can

One of D.C.’s buzziest theater companies opens a three-month, citywide festival of performances and exhibits celebrating “America's most enduring folk poet and social agitator.” Expect more than a “This Land Is Your Land” sing-along at this outdoor musical revue that addresses America’s turbulent social climate through the lens of Guthrie’s writings and songs. Recommended for fans of Bob Dylan, Pete Seeger and Rhiannon Giddens.

Rip! Tear! Collage Exhibit at Eye Street Gallery
200 I St. SE, 6 p.m. free

The D.C. Commission on the Arts and Humanities picked “Collage as Critique” as the theme for its annual juried show, which awards grants to artists whose work is chosen for display. More than 20 local artists have work in the 2026 exhibit, and three of them will be on hand to lead a workshop on shredding, tearing and ripping up paper, then turning the scraps into art.

More to explore: “Apollo 13” blasts off at the Library of Congress’ Movies on the Lawn.

Friday

“Tosca” at Wolf Trap
1551 Trap Road, Vienna, Va., 8 p.m., $39 to $107

The Washington National Opera Orchestra — a beleaguered group of veteran musicians who were recently kicked out of the Kennedy Center — will accompany up-and-coming singers on the Wolf Trap stage. The summer company produces one major opera each year, and this season it’s Puccini’s classic about an artist, his muse and the religious zealot police chief out to thwart their star-crossed romance. Husband-and-wife team Ryan and Tonya McKinny, who have vocally opposed President Trump’s Kennedy Center takeover, will direct the production and provide subtext, while José Luis Gómez conducts.

“SUNNY RAVE” at the Howard Theatre
620 T St., 10 p.m., $30

New York and Toronto may have “Heated Rivalry” parody musicals, but D.C. has [checks notes] a late-night “Always Sunny in Philadelphia” dance party? Yep. That’s a thing. The Philadelphia-based “dj pressed” will spin tunes accompanied by clips from the long-running FX comedy at the Howard Theatre. Come dressed as Mac, Dee or Danny DeVito.

More to explore: Country singer Jordan Davis performs a free show for ticketholders after the Nationals game.

Saturday

Chesapeake DogDocks at The Wharf
101 District Square SW, 10:30 a.m. to 6 p.m., free

Come watch Prince, Banana and their canine frenemies play fetch in a 40-foot pool installed outside The Anthem. Billed as the mid-Atlantic’s premiere “aquatic dog performance” club, the Chesapeake DockDogs are hosting their first District competition surrounded by bougie people drinking beer. (Cerveza Pacifico and Tito’s “Vodka for Dog People” are the event sponsors.) Think your pooch might have what it takes to take the big leap next year? The club is organizing a “Youth Day” introductory session in Marriottsville, Md., on Aug. 15, minus the pool and booze.

Crochet Community Social at Museum of Contemporary Art Arlington
525 14th St. S, Arlington, Va., 2:30 to 4 p.m., free

Bring your own needles or pick up a free pair at this informal gathering hosted by the Crochet Cart Project. Participants will each contribute a square for a community blanket. That may sound more wholesome than trad-wife Instagram, but the group also aims to spread the joy of crocheting to all communities and help people express “creativity through fibre art.”

More to explore: Swing Fling dance convention at the Dulles Hyatt Regency; Sneaker Con at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center.

Sunday

Summerfest Open House at Olney Theatre
2001 Olney-Sandy Spring Road, Olney, Md., 11:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., free

Families in the Northern suburbs (and anyone else who loves theater and has a car) are likely to love the grand opening of Olney Theatre Center’s multimillion-dollar expansion project. After two years of construction, the 88-year-old Montgomery County theater has a new lobby, studios and education spaces. More than two-dozen free shows, tours and workshops are on the schedule, while food trucks and a used costume shop are open all day. A gala performance featuring “Younger” star and Tony-winner Sutton Foster caps off the celebration, but tickets have long been sold out.

Mandoleers at Lyon Park Community Center
414 N. Fillmore Street, Arlington, Va., 5 p.m., free

Since 1923, the Mandoleers have been making music together on instruments that resemble miniature guitars. The ensemble holds a three-day intensive each summer, open to anyone who plays the mandolin, mandola, mandocello, classical guitar or upright bass. It’s unclear how exactly this merry band of musicians will celebrate the Declaration of Independence, but the event culminates with a free community concert called, “America at 250: We the People, All of Us.” Ernesto Parets conducts.

More to explore: Final weekend to see the critically hailed “American Aspirations” exhibit at the Smithsonian Institution Building.
